articles.title: New Bow Sonar Dome For Heavily Damaged Submarine USS Connecticut Seen For The First Time
articles.text:
TWZ has obtained new details about the ongoing repairs to the Seawolf class submarine USS Connecticut following collision with an underwater seamount in the South China Sea in 2021. The Navy had been looking at a roughly three-year timeline for the construction of a replacement bow sonar dome. In the end, it took just under a year for it to be built. The overall schedule for repairs to Connecticut has suffered delays, and we were the first to report that the boat is now not expected to return to service until next summer.

Janicki Industries produced the new bow sonar dome in approximately 10 months and delivered it to the Navy in 2024, the company told us today. Janicki has a history of producing “sonar domes and precision machined hardware” for U.S. nuclear submarine programs, according to its website. It has also supported various high-profile aerospace programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and F-35 Joint Strike Fighter.

Connecticut’s bow had initially remained attached, at least to some degree, following the collision five years ago, according to a heavily redacted Navy report on the accident. However, the entire bow structure subsequently broke away as the submarine limped to Guam. The boat then sailed to San Diego, California, and then to the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PSNS-IMF) in Washington State, where it has been ever since.

“Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & IMF [Intermediate Maintenance Facility] needed a precision replacement dome with no production line behind it, on the boat’s schedule,” Janicki also says on its website at the time of writing. “Janicki delivered it 24 months faster than the next-best option because everything the job needed sits under one roof: 5-axis mills that fit a hemisphere, the metrology to prove it, and the 1,000-ton press that forms double-curved plate.”

The picture seen in part at the top of this story and in full below shows one of Janicki proprietary five-axis milling machines at work on the dome.

The size and complexity of the bow sonar dome on Seawolf class submarines cannot be overstated. The bow sonar arrays on these boats is 24 feet in diameter. The structure of the dome itself has to be built to very exacting specifications for the sonar system to work properly.

Past Pentagon budget documents and appropriations bills from Congress had already highlighted the expected costs and complexities of replacing Connecticut’s bow sonar dome. In 2021, lawmakers approved $10 million in funding specifically for the dome, as well as $40 million for other “emergency repairs. The full repair bill is still unknown, but is expected to be far steeper than just $50 million.

In its Fiscal Year 2025 budget proposal, released in 2024, the Navy also outlined plans to acquire an additional bow dome in case any of its Seawolf class submarines suffered another similarly severe mishap.

“The Seawolf Class submarines sustainment strategy did not include the provisioning of replacement bow domes; therefore, no replacement bow domes for these in-service submarines are within the Navy’s inventory,” the budget documents explained. “This program would procure one Seawolf Class bow dome for use in the event replacement is required. Funds in FY25 are to purchase a bow dome which has a three plus year lead time.”

Note here the mention of a lead time of at least three years, which is in line with Janicki’s statement that the “next-best option” would have taken two years more to do this work.

As TWZ has highlighted in years of reporting now, repairs to Connecticut, in general, were always set to be challenging and costly due to the small size of the Seawolf class and the design being long out of production. The Navy originally planned to acquire 29 of these boats, but ultimately bought just three as a result of post-Cold War drawdowns. In addition, shrinking the program of record so severely caused the unit price of each one to rise substantially, just over $10 billion in 2025 dollars. At the time of writing, they are still the most costly attack submarines ever built. The last of the Seawolf class submarines, the highly secretive USS Jimmy Carter, which entered service in 2005, is also a heavily modified sub-type optimized for underwater espionage missions.

It is also worth noting that the U.S. Navy, as well as some of its foreign counterparts, have repaired similarly severe damage to submarines by cannibalizing entire sections from decommissioned boats in the same class. However, this is not an option given the size of the Seawolf class and the still very high demand for them operationally. The core design offers advanced capabilities that make even USS Seawolf and USS Connecticut especially well suited to a variety of specialized tasks. This is clearly why the Navy has continued to invest so much in returning Connecticut to the fleet.

As mentioned, repairs to Connecticut are now not expected to be finished until sometime in the summer of next year. This is the latest in a succession of schedule slips in recent years. The original goal had been for the boat to be back in service by September 2025.

“The Navy’s target completion date for the availability is the summer of 2027. PSNS & IMF is dedicated to executing this work with the highest standards of safety, technical accuracy, and craftsmanship to ensure the ship returns to the fleet ready to take its place at the tip of the spear in defense of our nation’s interests,” a Navy official told TWZ in September. “Current work consists of structural and systems restoration and required lifecycle maintenance.”

Earlier in the year, the Navy also revealed that it is now planning on sending Connecticut into retirement in 2031. This means the submarine has just four more years of service ahead of it if the current repair schedule holds.

The Navy does have plans to acquire a new class of nuclear attack submarines, currently referred to as SSN(X). In the past, the service has described those future boats as more of a direct successor to the Seawolf class than the versions of the Virginia class it is buying now.

“The analytical conclusion was unequivocal: to dominate high-end peer threats in the middle of this century, a clean sheet design is required. The Virginia class is a fantastic, unmatched world-class warship, and it will remain the backbone of our attack fleet for decades,” Navy Rear Adm. Andrew Miller, said at the Naval Submarine League’s main annual conference last week, per USNI News. “As adversary capabilities evolve, we require expanded payload capacity, greater electrical and hydrodynamic margins and unprecedented architectural flexibility that simply cannot be backfitted into an existing hull form.”

Miller is currently the head of the Undersea Warfare Division with the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations

In terms of desired key capabilities for SSN(X), the Navy wants “first, higher flank speed and tactical control speed. Two, improved operational availability. Three, decisive lethality. Four, superior stealth and layered survivability, and finally organic robotic and autonomous systems hosting and command and control,” Miller added. “We are redefining the role of the submarine from a standalone hunter-killer to a capital mothership. By launching uncrewed systems directly from submarine torpedo tubes and integrating unmanned [robotic] vehicles into our battle plans, we dramatically expand the tactical reach of our manned fleet.”

The first SSN(X) submarines are not expected to begin entering service until the mid-2040s, at the earliest. The Navy will continue acquiring Virginia class submarines in the interim. This includes stretched Block IV and V versions with Virginia Payload Modules (VPM) that will now be categorized as guided-missile types (SSGN). There will also be a one-of-a-kind seabed warfare version of the Virginia, which could well take over for the USS Jimmy Carter.

When it comes to USS Connecticut, if there are no further delays, the fully repaired submarine with its new bow sonar dome should be back in service by the middle of next year.

Contact the author: joe@twz.com

articles.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
articles.text:
Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence.

Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks.

In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys.

“Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday.

Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.

This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models.

In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks.

“The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote.

The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt.

In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.”

Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image.

While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote.

None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker.

“The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.”

The FBI weighs in

The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”

The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants.

After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October.

However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI.

The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert.

These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

articles.text:
The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.

articles.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
articles.text:
After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads.

“Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial. “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.”

The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard, the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself).

A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine

Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects.

The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids.

Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it.

While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well).

The Web’s about to get lit

Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas.

Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example, the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls, can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js, or to create charts with D3.js.

Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon.

Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas, then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code.

HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X.

A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath.

The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code.

Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas.

Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism.

“The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X.

Here be dragons

As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should, and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized.

And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn.

The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures.

Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

articles.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
articles.text:
A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind.

The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan.

But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs, each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz.

The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer, built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking.

Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger.

ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs.

Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64.

As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale.

In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame.

With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade.

Not the benchmark it used to be

The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them.

SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL.

It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor.

The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship.

It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time.

The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer.

The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them.

We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner.

It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI.

AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search.

High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®
articles.summary: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind.

Russia’s Prized Kerch Bridge Struck In Ukrainian Drone Onslaught
articles.text:
The Kerch Bridge, one of Russia’s most strategically important and heavily defended pieces of infrastructure, spanning the Kerch Strait between Krasnodar Krai in Russia and the Kerch Peninsula of Crimea, has been struck again. The latest attacks came amid a massive Ukrainian overnight offensive that Moscow says involved 1,336 long-range drones.

The Russian-installed head of occupied Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the crossing, which includes both automotive and rail lanes, had been targeted earlier today, announcing temporary traffic restrictions while authorities assessed the situation.

The attack reportedly occurred at approximately 5:38 a.m. local time, with a Ukrainian one-way attack drone striking one of the bridge’s arches. Russian air defenses were reportedly engaging incoming drones around the structure.

Video purportedly showing the moment of the attack includes the appearance of a straight-winged, propeller-driven drone with the twin booms and inverted-V tail that is a feature of several different Ukrainian strike drones.

The extent of the damage remains unclear, but there are now very visible signs of the main road span on the Kerch side of the bridge having been hit.

Footage broadcast on Russian television first showed the significant damage to the crossing. The main road span looks to have sustained a direct hit to its superstructure, with visible deformation of the structure. Reportedly, the original footage was subsequently removed by the Russian broadcaster.

One early report suggested that the affected arch was leaning at an approximately 15-degree angle. While certainly leaning, the precise angle has not been independently verified.

Meanwhile, satellite imagery confirms signs of damage to the bridge following the overnight attack, including around the arch of the road crossing, consistent with what we can see in the Russian television report. The imagery also appears to show dark marks, possibly scorch marks, at the opposite end of the main road span, although these may not be related to the latest attack.

Any kind of damage to the arch is noteworthy given the importance of the bridge’s supporting structure, although it is not yet possible to determine to what degree the structural elements impacted have been compromised.

Russian authorities were quick to indicate that traffic would resume following an inspection; the crossing remained closed long into the day. However, by the afternoon, Russian media were reporting that the bridge had reopened, albeit only in one direction at a time, although accompanying video footage appeared to deliberately avoid showing the damaged arch, and vehicles moving across the bridge were also absent from the available clip.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov characterized the damage as minor.

Nevertheless, approximately 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stranded in queues on either side of the crossing following the disruption. Rail services also experienced delays. It must also be taken into consideration that a partial reopening of the bridge to road traffic could also be a hubristic measure, and not necessarily a reflection of the true condition of the bridge structure.

The attack is particularly notable given the history of Ukrainian efforts to disable the bridge, which remains a critical logistical connection between Russia and the Crimean peninsula, illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014.

A recurring target for Ukraine

Ukraine’s sustained campaign against the Kerch crossing has involved several different methods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The first major attack occurred on October 8, 2022, when a truck carrying explosives detonated while crossing the bridge. The resulting blast damaged sections of the roadway and ignited fuel tankers aboard a train traveling across the adjacent railway span.

The attack temporarily disrupted traffic across the crossing and represented a significant security failure for Russian authorities. Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) subsequently acknowledged its involvement.

A second major attack followed on July 17, 2023, when Ukrainian forces employed domestically developed Sea Baby uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) against the bridge.

The naval drone attack damaged the road section, forcing another temporary closure. It also demonstrated Ukraine’s ability to threaten the crossing from the maritime domain despite the increasingly extensive defensive measures Russia had established around it.

Russia subsequently reinforced its defenses, deploying additional air defense systems and installing floating barriers, metal barges, and boom defenses intended to complicate attacks from the water.

Ukraine nevertheless demonstrated that the bridge remained vulnerable in June 2025, when the SBU carried out an underwater demolition operation targeting its support structures.

The agency said explosives equivalent to more than 1.1 metric tons of TNT had been detonated beneath the bridge following months of preparation. The SBU described the operation as having damaged underwater structural elements.

Part of a much larger drone offensive

The latest Kerch Bridge strike came amid what the Russian Ministry of Defense described as one of the largest Ukrainian drone attacks of the war.

The Russian Ministry of Defense claimed its air defenses intercepted or destroyed 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight across multiple regions, including occupied Crimea and areas around the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. The figure exceeds Moscow’s previous reported overnight interception record of 1,254 drones on October 29.

Russia subsequently reported a total of 2,049 drones intercepted over 24 hours, including the 1,336 overnight figure. Added to that total, per the same source, were four Flamingo cruise missiles and seven guided aerial bombs.

The actual number of drones launched by Ukraine is unknown, and the Russian claims have not been independently verified.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin separately claimed that approximately 600 drones had been directed towards the capital and surrounding region.

The reported barrage also affected industrial and energy infrastructure, with fires reported at several facilities in Russia’s Rostov region and elsewhere.

Again, these figures have not been independently verified and represent Russian official claims rather than a confirmed count of the total number of drones launched by Ukraine.

Nevertheless, the reported scale of the operation highlights the growing geographical reach of Ukraine’s long-range uncrewed attack campaign and the challenge facing Russian air defenses as they attempt to protect an expanding list of strategic sites.

The Kerch Bridge is an especially important target in this context. Beyond its enormous symbolic value as a signature infrastructure project associated with Russian President Vladimir Putin, it provides a major road and rail connection for moving military personnel, equipment, and supplies between mainland Russia and occupied Crimea.

Its disruption can therefore have consequences beyond the immediate damage to the structure itself, particularly if restrictions persist or repeated attacks force Russia to divert resources into its protection.

For Moscow, the latest incident also raises questions about the effectiveness of the defensive measures installed following the 2022 and 2023 attacks.

The massive overnight drone offensive also comes just days before an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen involving Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump, scheduled for November 19.

The meeting, taking place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, is expected to focus on broader issues of international security, including nuclear arms control and strategic stability. U.S. officials have indicated that Russia’s war against Ukraine is not expected to be featured in the trilateral discussions, despite Moscow’s interest in bringing the conflict to the table.

The timing nevertheless provides an important backdrop to the latest Ukrainian attacks. Kyiv continues to pursue a campaign against Russian military and strategic infrastructure while diplomatic efforts to end the nearly five-year war remain stalled.

For Putin, the summit offers an opportunity for direct engagement with Trump and Xi at a time when Russia’s military campaign in Ukraine continues to face significant challenges. The latest drone barrage, meanwhile, underscores Ukraine’s ability to bring the war to targets deep inside Russia, including infrastructure with considerable strategic and symbolic importance.

Whether Monday’s reported strike caused more significant structural damage to the Kerch Bridge remains uncertain, although initial imagery certainly seems to point toward that. The results of this attack may well also encourage Ukraine to immediately do whatever it can to retarget and strike that exact weakened point in an attempt to deal a more fatal blow to the bridge.

articles.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
articles.text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. 

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. 

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. 

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

articles.title: ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years
articles.text:
It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime.

NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way.

“Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.”

Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either.

According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place.

“We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present.

AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised.

The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA.

But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example.

Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends.

“Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years.

The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said.

We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

articles.title: NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making
articles.text:
The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it.

Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine.

The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it.

Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs.

Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it.

Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes.

Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx.

Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready.

His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server.

In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service.

A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5.

For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue.

Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces.

Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

articles.title: Ubuntu gets AI-generated security fixes for those feeling brave
articles.text:
Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering.

Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive, an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework.

As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive."

Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated.

Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company.

At the previous such event in June, the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious.

The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team.

It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism).

It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022, Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings.

We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30, surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world.

Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money. ®

articles.title: Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage
articles.text:
Microsoft has released an out-of-band update to fix licensing and activation errors introduced by November's Windows security update.

The fix is available from the Microsoft Update Catalog for Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019, Windows 10 22H2 ESU, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 and 2019. Windows 11 23H2 users can obtain it from the Catalog or through Windows Update's Optional updates menu.

The "non-security OOB update" targets affected enterprise devices. Microsoft stated: "Certain Windows licensing and activation operations using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail with error 0x80041008 (Invalid parameter).

"This primarily affects organizations using slmgr.vbs commands or automated processes to configure Key Management Service (KMS) activation, install product keys, or manage Windows licensing."

Devices that are already activated will remain activated, Microsoft said.

Breaking the machinery customers use to activate paid-for software is a bad look for a Patch Tuesday release. Administrators may wonder how Microsoft's updates are tested when installing one means waiting for another to repair the damage.

Those same administrators may also have been fielding calls about last week's widespread Exchange Online outage, which Microsoft has partly attributed to a defect it introduced in July.

On top of that, Microsoft told administrators just days ago to consider unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 "permanently vulnerable." Exchange Online avoids that particular support deadline, but the recent outage was a reminder that handing over the servers doesn't make software defects disappear.

Forget "security by obscurity." Last week's approach was more like "security by unavailability."

Between getting Windows activated and keeping Exchange Online online, Microsoft gave administrators plenty to do. None of it was likely to feature in their original plans for the week.

Not all the glitches introduced by November's Patch Tuesday have yet been resolved, as some customers using a Windows device to print will be aware. ®

articles.title: Crook turns free trials into phishing factory, as LearnWorlds sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
articles.text:
LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to customers over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached.

Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to customers.

"We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register.

According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails.

"In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address."

The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes.

LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14.

"In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14.

"We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list."

The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags.

"We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined.

"Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity."

The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content.

Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame, who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server.

The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X, referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.”

The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts.

“The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.”

According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same.

Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks.

These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it.

LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue.

The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

articles.title: PM Modi to Attend ASEAN-India and East Asia Summits in Philippines
articles.text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi embarked on his visit to the Philippines on Monday to attend the 23rd Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-India Summit and the 21st meeting of the ASEAN-led East Asia Summit process.
The Prime Minister expressed confidence that the visit will infuse new energy in the bilateral partnership with ASEAN and reinforce the commitment to a “peaceful, prosperous and resilient Indo-Pacific”.
In his departure statement, PM Modi said, “Today, I am embarking on a visit to Manila to participate in the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit on 17 November 2026, at the invitation of President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.”
“Our relationship with ASEAN countries is at the heart of India’s Act East Policy and occupies a central place in our MAHASAGAR vision. Our ties, rooted in centuries of civilisational exchanges, have grown into a dynamic partnership spanning trade, connectivity, maritime security, technology and people-to-people relations,” he said.
The Prime Minister further stated that he looks forward to working with the ASEAN leaders to “build on the progress of our Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and give further momentum to our shared aspirations for growth, connectivity and prosperity” during the ASEAN-India Summit.
He said that the East Asia Summit provides an “important platform for dialogue on regional and global challenges”.
“I look forward to exchanging views with participating leaders on strengthening peace, stability and cooperation in the Indo-Pacific,” he said.
PM Modi will also interact with the Indian diaspora in the Philippines.
“I also look forward to interacting with the vibrant Indian community in the Philippines, whose contributions strengthen the bonds of friendship between our two countries,” he said.
“I am confident that the visit will impart new energy to India’s partnership with ASEAN and reinforce our collective commitment to a peaceful, prosperous and resilient Indo-Pacific,” the Prime Minister added.
PM Modi’s programme in Manila will include a dinner hosted by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for the visiting dignitaries, followed by the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit the next day, with bilateral meetings with other leaders in between.
The visit comes as India and ASEAN are celebrating 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation, and will commemorate 35 years of Dialogue Relations and five years of our Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2027.
According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), India-ASEAN relations are a central pillar of India’s Act East Policy and our vision for the Indo-Pacific.
“The ASEAN-India Summit will review progress in the implementation of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, including the ASEAN-India Plan of Action 2026–2030, and chart the future direction of cooperation,” the Ministry said.
It further stated that the East Asia Summit will provide an opportunity to deliberate on matters of regional and global importance with ASEAN and other participating countries.
(IANS)

Nvidia earnings spotlight shifts to leadership, AI financing after Huang exit
articles.text: The sudden departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has transformed the focus of the chipmaker’s quarterly earnings from margins and cash deployment to broader questions about its leadership and influence across the artificial intelligence industry, Reuters reported.Huang stepped down last Thursday following revelations about extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected of spying for China. His exit plunged Nvidia into a leadership crisis and unsettled an AI ecosystem that the company helped finance.Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, while Nvidia’s board has said it is selecting a firm to lead the search for a permanent successor. The company is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the market closes on Tuesday.Before Huang’s departure, investors were focused on Nvidia’s falling market value, whether debt-funded AI spending could continue into 2027 and whether its high profit margins were sustainable.For live updates on US Markets, click hereAttention has now shifted to whether Kress can reassure investors that Nvidia will maintain its technological lead while continuing to support cloud providers, suppliers and AI laboratories through investments and financial guarantees. Analysts are also likely to ask whether Huang could return as CEO.“The earnings itself should be typical, but any comfort we can get on the rest of the business and the management changes is probably the most important piece,” Brian Colello, technology equity analyst at Morningstar Research Services told Reuters.“We’ll want any early insights on what Nvidia will do in the interim, what they’re seeing with customers, what they’re seeing with partnerships, finance, government, a lot of questions there. I don’t know if we’ll get many answers, but we’ll want to at least hear the company’s statements on those sort of things.”Nvidia, valued at about $4 trillion and until recently the world’s most valuable company, has consistently exceeded analysts’ expectations.Also Read | Michael Burry warns of 'mild manipulation' in Nvidia's China sales. What Big Short investor expects for the stockRevenue more than doubled from a year earlier in the second quarter ended July, while gross margins reached 75%. The company returned $26 billion to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks.Nvidia subsequently forecast third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, and projected 70% growth next year. It also warned that higher memory costs would weigh on gross margins.Adjusted profit for the October quarter is expected to reach $2.47 per share, up from $1.30 a year earlier.Despite its strong results, Nvidia’s share price has fallen by about a third from its October peak. Its price-to-earnings ratio has dropped to 11 from as high as 40 eight months ago.“The multiple has been under pressure even prior to Huang’s departure. The market is evidently sceptical of those earnings’ growth expectations,” Rory Dowie, a London-based equity portfolio manager at Marlborough, told Reuters.“We do believe that Huang’s departure puts those earnings more at risk. We prefer to be positioned in the companies looking to take share out of the Nvidia pie. Huang departing perhaps pushes the door a bit more open for the likes of AMD or Broadcom,” he said.Key numbers in focusDan Morgan, a portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, expects Nvidia’s third-quarter revenue to exceed the consensus estimate of $109.08 billion by between $2 billion and $3 billion. That would represent year-over-year growth of more than 90%, as per Reuters report.However, Morgan said the bigger question was “what does Nvidia need to do to shake off the abundance of uncertainties circling the company to allow the stock  to break out of the current trading range?”Investors will closely watch the contribution from Nvidia’s new Vera Rubin data-centre platform and whether Rubin graphics processors account for a projected one-fifth of third-quarter revenue.Another major issue is whether Nvidia will maintain the extensive financing arrangements that Kress is believed to have opposed. The deals include investments in OpenAI and AI infrastructure companies such as Lambda and have contributed to concerns among some Wall Street critics about a potentially circular AI economy.Some estimates put Nvidia’s commitments at more than half a trillion dollars across supply and capacity guarantees for chip purchases, data-centre leases and equity investments. The total nevertheless remains a fraction of the company’s market value.Max Anderl, a hedge-fund manager at SilverSea Asset Management, said investors were also concerned about Nvidia’s use of cash. He noted that nearly a third of the company’s profits were non-operating, suggesting they were partly driven by changes in the market value of its equity investments.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
articles.text:
Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.

Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania's health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state's seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.

For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they're the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania's case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

SpaceX Makes Historic Launch Tower Catch of Returning Starship
articles.text:
SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for – the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss.
“Can you believe it?” shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
The world’s largest and most powerful rocket – a 407-foot (124-metre) behemoth – blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the US-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
articles.text:
Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration, signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities.

Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy.

But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains."

The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together."

It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains."

This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants."

Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon.

The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom.

"The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times.

"What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility."

This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing.

It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms.

American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration, and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership.

A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs.

It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

articles.title: Rajasthan Train Blast Case: Punjab Woman Held Over Alleged Terror Plot
articles.text:
A romantic relationship allegedly became the entry point to a terror conspiracy aimed at derailing a passenger train in Rajasthan. A Pakistani handler reportedly lured a divorced woman into a ‘love trap’, promised her money and recruited her to plant explosives on a railway track. She, in turn, allegedly involved her boyfriend by promising him money and marriage.
The Anti-Terrorist Squad (ATS) has arrested two suspects, including a 21-year-old woman, in connection with the November 3 blast on the Anupgarh-Suratgarh railway line in Sri Ganganagar district.
The accused allegedly received Rs 2.23 lakh from their Pakistani handlers and were trained through video calls to plant and detonate improvised explosive devices (IEDs).
ATS Additional Director General Dinesh M.N. said the conspiracy was allegedly orchestrated at the direction of Pakistan’s ISI, with the objective of blowing up a passenger train. However, a timing error meant that the explosives detonated nearly 30 minutes after the train had passed, averting a possible major disaster.
The ATS arrested Mahakdeep Kaur (21) and Devendra Singh (23), both residents of Gurdaspur in Punjab. They were produced before the Additional Civil Judge and Judicial Magistrate No. 2 on Sunday and remanded to eight days of police custody.
According to the ATS investigation, Mahakdeep’s alleged involvement began through a contact provided by her former husband, Karan.
Mahakdeep had married Karan around two years ago, but the marriage ended in divorce on December 24, 2024. In February 2025, Karan was jailed in a heroin smuggling case. During a visit to the prison, he allegedly gave Mahakdeep the phone number of a Pakistani-based smuggler known as Lovely, through whom she could arrange money.
Mahakdeep subsequently established contact with Lovely, who introduced her to an associate identified as Shah. The latter allegedly cultivated a romantic relationship with her and gradually persuaded her to carry out an explosion on a railway track in return for money.
Shah then allegedly introduced Mahakdeep and her boyfriend, Devendra, to another Pakistani-based associate, described as his uncle, through a video call. The handler assigned them the task of planting an IED and later provided instructions through video calls on preparing and setting a time bomb.
Investigators said Mahakdeep brought Devendra into the conspiracy. The two had known each other since their Class 12 days and were reportedly in a relationship.
According to the ATS, Mahakdeep promised Devendra money and marriage to persuade him to participate in the operation. The Pakistani handler allegedly paid the couple a total of Rs 2.23 lakh, including Rs 1 lakh in cash and the remaining amount through online transfers. The couple was also allegedly given instructions about where to collect the explosives and how to plant them on the railway track.
The ATS said the two suspects first travelled to Vijaynagar in Sri Ganganagar district on October 6 to collect explosives from a designated location. However, they returned empty-handed after failing to find the consignment. They reportedly returned to the region on October 12-13 and planted two time bombs on the railway track between Ramsinghpur and Vijaynagar. However, the explosives did not detonate because of broken wires and technical problems.
After contacting a local person to ascertain whether the blast had occurred, they realised that the attempt had failed. When they informed their Pakistani handler, he allegedly reprimanded them. The third attempt was made on November 3.
The accused reportedly arrived in Sri Ganganagar on October 30 and stayed at a hotel. According to investigators, they subsequently collected explosives delivered through a drone drop near the Punjab border.
After failing to execute the plan on November 1 and 2, they allegedly planted a time bomb near 50 GB village on the evening of November 3 and fled towards Punjab. At around 9.45 p.m., a powerful explosion rocked the railway track. The blast created a crater between the tracks and damaged two railway sleepers, disrupting train movement for nearly 10 hours. The train had already passed the spot by the time the explosives detonated.
Dinesh M.N. said the ATS analysed more than five lakh mobile data records and over 200 CCTV clips to identify the suspects. With assistance from the Amritsar CI Cell and Gurdaspur SP, the team eventually traced and arrested the duo in the Kalanaur police station area in Punjab.
During the operation, investigators recovered Rs 30,000 in cash, two foreign-made pistols and 40 cartridges bearing the stamp of the Pakistan Ordnance Factory.
The ATS also suspects that the network is part of a wider recruitment strategy being used by Pakistan-based operatives.
According to Dinesh M.N., an individual identified as Shahzad Bhatti emerged as an active threat following Operation Sindoor and has allegedly been targeting Indian youth through a model involving monetary inducements and online instructions for carrying out criminal activities.
The ADG said the handlers were particularly targeting divorced or single women, using romantic overtures and financial promises to draw them into their network.
He cited another case involving a divorced woman, Babita, who was allegedly approached in a similar manner and subsequently arrested by the ATS.
Bikaner IG Omprakash and Sri Ganganagar SP Harishankar said Pakistan-based handlers were exploiting linguistic, cultural and family connections between the border districts of Punjab and Rajasthan. Districts such as Gurdaspur, Tarn Taran and Fazilka share cultural and linguistic similarities with Sri Ganganagar, making it easier for handlers to establish contact with local residents, police officials said.
Investigators are also questioning the cab driver who allegedly transported the accused during their movements in the region. Families say they knew nothing about the alleged activities. While investigators piece together the alleged terror network, the families of the two arrested suspects have expressed shock, claiming they were unaware of their activities.
Mahakdeep’s mother, Sarabjit Kaur, said her daughter had completed her education up to Class 12 and had married of her own choice before the relationship ended in divorce. Her father, Tirlok Singh, said the family learnt about her alleged involvement only when the police arrived at their house.
Devendra’s mother, Baljit Kaur, and aunt, Sukhwinder Kaur, said he had also studied up to Class 12 and was in a relationship with Mahakdeep.
According to his aunt, Devendra left home two days before the November 3 blast, saying he was going to Delhi. He returned three days after the explosion.
She claimed Mahakdeep had promised him Rs 1 lakh, which he was allegedly going to collect. His mother, however, recalled that he had told the family he was going to Amritsar to bring a motorcycle. He returned home on November 7-8, following which the police arrived and took him into custody.
The families’ accounts have added another dimension to the investigation, which is now examining how personal relationships, financial inducements and online communication were allegedly used to recruit young people into a cross-border conspiracy.
The ATS is continuing its investigation to establish the complete network, identify the handlers and trace the movement of explosives and money.
