articles.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
articles.text:
In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Where traditional definitions of trust fall short

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

Building trust that scales

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.

Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

  1. What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
  2. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.
  3. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
  4. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
  5. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

articles.title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
articles.text:
October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application.

Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet.

Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded.

A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work.

In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100.

These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first.

Security has to become every developer’s responsibility

Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them.

Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do.

A new approach to securing your code

CodeRabbit Secure uses semantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes.

Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC:

  • reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks;

  • finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan;

  • rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime.

Find vulnerabilities already in committed code

Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it.

I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable.

Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep

Review incoming changes before merge

PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application.

CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff.

On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved.

Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime

Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them.

For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed.

Carry the investigation through to a fix

Developers can ask CodeRabbit Agent to implement a fix and open a PR, then inspect the finding, proposed fix, and supporting evidence. Teams can also configure severity thresholds to create Jira or Linear tickets automatically and track remediation in their existing workflow.

Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file.

What a million-dollar initiative surfaced

CodeRabbit recently committed up to $1 million in free Deep Scans to help organizations find and fix hidden vulnerabilities. In Deep Scans created over a 10-day period in early November, CodeRabbit Secure recorded about 53,000 High or Critical findings across some 2,000 organizations. More than 10,000 findings have already been fixed, including 1,049 rated High or Critical.

Some of the security fixes implemented by CodeRabbit included preventing:

  • embedded JavaScript in a repository document’s metadata from running arbitrary code.

  • email subject lines from being interpreted as executable templates and running JavaScript with an API server’s privileges.

  • unauthenticated transfer requests from injecting SQL and triggering unauthorized database operations.

As agents produce more code and attackers become more capable, investigation using semantic analysis needs to become a regular part of how software is built and maintained, alongside existing security checks.

Find vulnerabilities in your code before an attacker does

As attackers use AI agents to investigate unfamiliar systems and adapt their next move, engineering and security teams need the same capacity to investigate their code and carry findings through to tested fixes.

articles.title: IAF’s Unusual Night Vision Requirement Points to a Specialised Surveillance Need
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force has released an intriguing procurement requirement for an advanced night vision system to be used at Air Force Station Sirsa. The requirement is far more advanced than just simple night vision goggles. It can be found on the Government e-Marketplace here . The requirement is for a night vision system with 10x optical zoom and long range infrared observation and tracking capabilities.
The requirement is for a system with 10x optical zoom and claims to offer between 650-700 meters range with active infrared illumination. It must also provide over 1200 meters of tracking range and use an 850nm infrared illuminator.
This suggests that the IAF aren’t looking for simple night vision goggles but a system capable of identifying, observing and tracking objects much further away.
An active infrared system uses an IR illuminator to emit the energy that can then be picked up by an appropriate sensor. This means you can create an image when there isn’t enough ambient light. A passive night vision system doesn’t use any active components.
The fact that this system must offer over 1200 meters of passive tracking range is interesting as it means that if it is used to observe objects it can do so from a large distance without using any active IR sources. This can be useful in a military context to reduce the signature of the system.
The system must also use an 850nm Infrared illuminator. This means that it will be emitting energy in the Near Infrared region of the spectrum. This means that it will be able to be picked up by appropriate night vision systems but is mostly not visible to the naked eye. It can offer the operator a much greater night vision capability than they would have without any assistance.
Although this may suggest that it’s being procured as some form of pilot mounted night vision goggles, the tracking range and 10x optical zoom suggest that this could be a specialist system for observation or surveillance. The exact purpose of this system will depend on the full details of the tender, how many are being procured and what else is required.
Air Force Station Sirsa is an important part of the Indian Air Force and is located in Haryana. They have been known to run transport and helicopter operations. This specialist night vision equipment could be used for a variety of purposes on Airbases such as security, surveillance, night operations and other roles where people need to see or track objects in poor lighting. However, this tender doesn’t specify what aircraft/squadron/unit this will be used for.
This does reflect a trend in modern militaries. Electro Optical sensors are becoming increasingly important in providing situational awareness at night. Modern night vision systems can include image intensifiers, IR sensors, zoom lenses and digital processing to provide valuable information.
The IAF could use this system for a number of purposes. Airbase security, security, maintenance and other ground based roles can all benefit from this type of system.
The most interesting aspect of this tender is the tracking capability. It needs to be able to passively track objects over 1200 meters away. If it can meet this requirement it would offer a large night vision capability. How well it performs will depend on the atmospheric conditions, how much ambient light there is, how big the objects are, how sensitive the sensor is and the quality of the optics.
Overall, this is an interesting procurement (GEM/2026/B/7851051) as it suggests that the IAF wants more than simple night vision. They want a system with zoom, passive long range viewing and an active IR illuminator.

articles.title: AMCA Production Partner Winner Likely by December
articles.text:
India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) may soon see a crucial decision, as Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said that the winner to be selected as the development and production partner can be declared within a month. He also confirmed that all three shortlisted firms have submitted their proposals.
“In a month’s time, we will be ready to announce the winner of the race,” Singh told ANI National Security Summit 3.0 in New Delhi on November 16. The selection would speed up the development of AMCA prototypes, he added.
This would mean the winner being selected in December 2026. The development and production partner agreement would then be finalised after the evaluation, discussions, and signing of the deal which could happen in March 2027. Tata Advanced Systems is bidding alone while Larsen & Toubro have partnered with Bharat Electronics Limited and Dynamatic Technologies. Bharat Forge is leading the third team, in partnership with BEML and Data Patterns.
The selection is important because the winning company/consortium will work with the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA). The design of the plane will remain with the ADA, however the partner will play a large role in developing the aircraft. The partner will also be responsible for setting up the manufacturing base.
The first phase of the project includes building five flying prototypes and one structural test article. The estimate of the cost to develop the prototypes is around ₹15,000 crore, however this will depend on the final contractual agreements. The selection process has taken longer than anticipated, with the proposal deadline having been pushed back. Now the next step will be to evaluate the proposals and finalise an agreement with the partner. March 2027 would be a big milestone, but it is not the beginning of operations. The partner will need to set up the necessary facilities first.

articles.title: Jensen Huang allies build a "war room" to get him back at Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the company’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

articles.title: Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
articles.text:
Mercedes-Benz provided flights from Washington, DC, to San Francisco and accommodation so Ars could try its new driver assistance systems. Ars does not accept paid editorial content.

SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.

Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days.
